stem: The Harappan Civilisation is also known as the __________ Civilisation, after the river valley where many of its sites were first found.
solution: The Harappan Civilisation is also known as the Indus Valley Civilisation, because many of its major sites were located in the valley of the river Indus (and its tributaries) — in the north-western part of the Indian subcontinent (in present-day Pakistan and north-western India). It is called 'Harappan' after Harappa, the first site to be discovered/excavated (in the 1920s). It was one of the world's earliest urban (city-based) civilisations. Understanding the alternative name (Indus Valley Civilisation) and its basis is a fundamental prelims point. The Harappan Civilisation is also called the Indus Valley Civilisation, after the Indus river valley where many of its sites lay.

stem: The Harappan Civilisation is named after the site of __________, which was the first to be discovered/excavated.
solution: The civilisation is called the 'Harappan Civilisation' after the site of Harappa (in present-day Punjab, Pakistan), which was the first of its sites to be discovered and excavated (in the 1920s). It is a convention in archaeology to name a civilisation/culture after the first site where its distinctive artefacts were found — so this civilisation is named after Harappa. (The term 'Harappan' is also used because the civilisation extended well beyond the Indus valley, so 'Indus Valley' is somewhat narrow.) Understanding that the civilisation is named after Harappa (the first-discovered site) is a prelims point. The Harappan Civilisation is named after Harappa, the first of its sites to be discovered/excavated.

stem: The Harappan Civilisation is dated to approximately (the 'Mature Harappan' phase):
solution: The Mature Harappan phase — the phase of the great cities and full urban civilisation — is dated to approximately 2600 BCE to 1900 BCE (i.e., roughly 4,600 to 3,900 years ago). (There were 'Early Harappan' cultures before c. 2600 BCE, and 'Late Harappan' cultures after c. 1900 BCE, when the civilisation declined.) So the Harappan Civilisation flourished in the third millennium BCE, making it one of the world's earliest (Bronze Age) urban civilisations, contemporary with those of Mesopotamia and Egypt. Understanding the date of the Mature Harappan phase (c. 2600–1900 BCE) is a key prelims point. The Mature Harappan phase is dated to approximately 2600–1900 BCE.

stem: A distinctive feature of Harappan cities (like Mohenjodaro) was their careful __________, with streets laid out in a grid pattern.
solution: A distinctive and remarkable feature of the Harappan cities (like Mohenjodaro and Harappa) was their careful town planning. The cities were laid out on a planned grid pattern — with streets and lanes running in straight lines and crossing one another at right angles (dividing the city into rectangular blocks). This shows a high degree of civic organisation and planning (a municipal authority). The planned layout, along with the drainage system and standardised bricks, reflects the advanced urban character of the Harappan Civilisation. Understanding the grid-pattern town planning of Harappan cities is a key prelims point. Harappan cities had careful town planning, with streets laid out in a grid pattern.

stem: Harappan cities were typically divided into two parts: a higher, walled part (the 'Citadel') and a lower, larger part called the:
solution: Harappan cities (like Mohenjodaro) were typically divided into two distinct parts: (1) the 'Citadel' — a higher, smaller, walled part, built on a raised platform (mud-brick), which contained important public buildings and structures (like the Great Bath and the granary at Mohenjodaro); and (2) the 'Lower Town' — a larger, lower part, where most of the residential/ordinary buildings (houses) were located. This division into a raised Citadel and a Lower Town is a characteristic feature of Harappan urban layout. Understanding the Citadel and Lower Town division is a key prelims point. Harappan cities were divided into a higher walled 'Citadel' and a lower, larger 'Lower Town'.

stem: The most famous structure of the Citadel at Mohenjodaro, a large watertight tank possibly used for ritual bathing, is the:
solution: The most famous structure at Mohenjodaro is the 'Great Bath' — a large, rectangular, watertight tank (pool), located in the Citadel, made of finely-fitted bricks made watertight with a lining of gypsum mortar (and bitumen/tar). It had steps leading down into it on two sides, and rooms around it. It was most likely used for some kind of special ritual bathing (a religious/ceremonial purpose). The Great Bath is remarkable evidence of the Harappans' engineering skill and probably their ritual practices. Understanding the Great Bath (at Mohenjodaro) is a key prelims point. The Great Bath at Mohenjodaro is a large watertight tank, probably used for ritual bathing.

stem: A remarkable feature of Harappan cities was their well-planned __________ system, with covered drains along the streets.
solution: A remarkable and advanced feature of the Harappan cities was their well-planned drainage (sanitation) system. Almost every house had drains, which were connected to larger covered drains running along the streets; the drains were built of bricks, were covered (with removable brick slabs or stones, for cleaning), and were laid with a gradient/slope so the water flowed. This careful arrangement for carrying away waste water and sewage — one of the most sophisticated of any ancient civilisation — reflects a high concern for cleanliness/sanitation and a high level of civic planning and organisation. Understanding the Harappan drainage system is a key prelims point. Harappan cities had a well-planned drainage system, with covered drains running along the streets.

stem: The Harappans built their houses, drains, and structures using standardised __________ (of a fixed ratio), showing standardisation.
solution: The Harappans built their houses, walls, drains, and other structures using standardised bricks — often baked/burnt bricks (and also sun-dried mud bricks). Remarkably, these bricks were of a standardised size, made to a fixed ratio (the length being twice the breadth, and the breadth twice the height — a 4:2:1 ratio), and this same ratio/standard was used across the far-flung Harappan sites. This standardisation of bricks (over such a wide area) is striking evidence of a high degree of standardisation, organisation, and perhaps central regulation in the Harappan Civilisation. Understanding the standardised Harappan bricks is a prelims point. The Harappans used standardised (baked) bricks of a fixed ratio, showing remarkable standardisation.

stem: A large brick structure at the Mohenjodaro Citadel, thought to have been used to store grain, is called the:
solution: At the Citadel of Mohenjodaro (and also at Harappa), there is a large brick structure that archaeologists have identified as a 'granary' (or warehouse) — a building thought to have been used for the storage of grain (food grains). The existence of such large storage structures suggests that the Harappans collected and stored surplus grain (perhaps as tax/tribute, or for redistribution or trade), which in turn points to an organised system of agriculture, surplus, and administration. (The identification as a 'granary' is an interpretation, not certain.) Understanding the Harappan granary is a prelims point. The large brick structure at the Mohenjodaro Citadel, thought to store grain, is called the granary.

stem: The Harappans had a system of writing (a script), which is found on their seals. However, this Harappan script:
options: has NOT yet been deciphered (its meaning is still unknown)
solution: The Harappans did have a system of writing — a script — which is found inscribed on their seals, and also on copper tablets, pottery, and other objects. However, the Harappan script has NOT yet been deciphered — that is, scholars have not been able to read/understand it (its meaning remains unknown). The script consists of signs/symbols (pictographs), and it was probably written from right to left. Because it is undeciphered, we cannot read the Harappans' own writings, which is a major reason so much about them remains a mystery (we depend on archaeological evidence rather than written records). Understanding that the Harappan script is undeciphered is a key prelims point. The Harappans had a script (found on seals), but it has not yet been deciphered.

stem: The Harappans made distinctive __________, usually made of steatite (a soft stone), often engraved with animals and script, probably used in trade.
solution: The Harappans made distinctive seals — small, usually square objects, most commonly made of steatite (a soft stone) — which are among the most characteristic artefacts of the civilisation. The seals were typically engraved with an animal (like the 'unicorn', the humped bull, the elephant, etc.) and with a line of the (undeciphered) Harappan script. The seals were probably used in trade — for example, to stamp/seal goods and bundles (marking ownership or authenticating), and perhaps for administrative purposes. They are a key source of evidence about the Harappans (their art, animals, script, and trade). Understanding the Harappan seals (steatite, with animals and script) is a key prelims point. The Harappans made distinctive seals of steatite, engraved with animals and script, probably used in trade.

stem: The most commonly depicted animal on the Harappan seals is a mythical one-horned creature usually called the:
solution: The animal most frequently/commonly depicted on the Harappan seals is a mythical one-horned creature usually called the 'unicorn' (a bull-like animal shown in profile with a single horn). The unicorn appears on a very large number of seals. (Other animals depicted include the humped bull, the elephant, the rhinoceros, the tiger, and the buffalo.) The frequent appearance of the unicorn suggests it may have had a special significance (perhaps religious or symbolic). Understanding that the unicorn is the most common animal on the seals is a prelims point. The most commonly depicted animal on the Harappan seals is the (mythical) 'unicorn'.

stem: The Harappan economy was based on agriculture, craft production, and __________ (with distant places like Mesopotamia).
solution: The Harappan economy was based on: agriculture (they grew crops like wheat, barley, pulses, and cotton, and reared animals); craft production (they were skilled in making beads, seals, pottery, metal tools, and ornaments); and trade (both internal and external/long-distance). They traded over long distances — importantly, there is evidence of trade contacts with Mesopotamia (in West Asia), where Harappan seals and goods have been found, and Mesopotamian texts refer to a land called 'Meluhha' (which many scholars identify with the Harappan region). The Harappans traded goods like beads, cotton, and possibly other items. So trade (including with distant Mesopotamia) was an important part of the Harappan economy. Understanding the trade-based Harappan economy (including with Mesopotamia) is a prelims point. The Harappan economy included agriculture, crafts, and trade — including long-distance trade with Mesopotamia.

stem: Mesopotamian texts refer to a distant land called '__________', which many scholars identify with the Harappan region.
solution: Mesopotamian texts (from West Asia) refer to a distant land called 'Meluhha', with which the Mesopotamians traded — obtaining goods such as carnelian beads, wood, and other items. Many scholars identify Meluhha with the Harappan region (the Indus Valley Civilisation), based on the trade evidence (Harappan goods found in Mesopotamia, and the descriptions matching). This reference is important evidence of the long-distance trade contacts between the Harappan Civilisation and Mesopotamia. Understanding the identification of Meluhha with the Harappan region is a prelims point. Mesopotamian texts refer to a land called 'Meluhha', which many scholars identify with the Harappan region.

stem: The Harappans were skilled craftsmen, especially known for making beautiful __________ (from materials like carnelian, agate, and steatite).
solution: The Harappans were highly skilled craftsmen, and they were especially renowned for making beautiful beads and ornaments — from a variety of materials such as carnelian (a reddish stone), agate, jasper, steatite, shell, faience (a glassy material), copper, gold, and terracotta. Bead-making was an important and specialised craft (e.g., at sites like Chanhudaro and Lothal), and the finely-made beads (including long, barrel-shaped carnelian beads) were both used locally and traded (some reaching Mesopotamia). The Harappans also made pottery, seals, metal tools, and jewellery. Understanding the Harappans' skill in bead/ornament-making is a prelims point. The Harappans were skilled at making beautiful beads and ornaments from materials like carnelian, agate, and steatite.

stem: The famous bronze statuette of a girl, an example of Harappan art (made by the lost-wax technique), is called the:
solution: The famous bronze statuette of a girl found at Mohenjodaro is called the 'Dancing Girl'. It is a small bronze figure of a young girl in a confident, relaxed pose (with one hand on her hip), made by the 'lost-wax' (cire perdue) technique of metal casting. It is one of the most celebrated examples of Harappan art and metalwork, demonstrating the Harappans' skill in bronze casting. (Another famous Harappan sculpture is the stone bust known as the 'Priest-King'.) Understanding the 'Dancing Girl' bronze is a prelims point. The famous Harappan bronze statuette of a girl is called the 'Dancing Girl'.

stem: Unlike some other ancient civilisations, the Harappan Civilisation has NOT provided clear evidence of __________ (like large temples, royal tombs, or grand palaces of kings).
options: monumental religious or royal structures / a clearly-identified ruling authority
solution: Unlike some other ancient civilisations (such as Egypt, with its pyramids/royal tombs and grand temples, or Mesopotamia), the Harappan Civilisation has NOT provided clear evidence of monumental religious or royal structures — there are no clearly-identified large temples, grand palaces, or royal tombs, and no obvious images/records of kings or rulers. This absence has puzzled scholars and led to debate about how the Harappan society was organised and who ruled it (whether there were kings, a group of rulers, or some other kind of authority). The lack of ostentatious royal/religious monuments is a distinctive (and mysterious) feature of the Harappan Civilisation. Understanding this (absence of clear temples/palaces/royal tombs) is a prelims point. The Harappan Civilisation lacks clear evidence of monumental temples, palaces, or royal tombs (or an identified ruling authority).

stem: The Harappan site of __________ (in Gujarat, India) is notable for its dockyard, suggesting it was a port for maritime trade.
solution: Lothal, a Harappan site in Gujarat (India), is notable for its dockyard — a large brick structure identified as a dock (for berthing and servicing ships/boats). This suggests that Lothal was an important port town, engaged in maritime (sea) trade. Lothal was also a centre of bead-making and other crafts. The dockyard at Lothal is important evidence of the Harappans' seafaring and trade. (Other important Harappan sites in India include Kalibangan, Dholavira, Rakhigarhi, and Banawali.) Understanding that Lothal (Gujarat) had a dockyard/was a port is a prelims point. Lothal, in Gujarat, is notable for its dockyard, suggesting it was a port for maritime trade.

stem: The decline of the Harappan Civilisation (around 1900 BCE) is attributed by scholars to various possible causes, but NOT clearly to any single one. Which is a proposed cause?
options: Climatic/environmental change (drying up of rivers, deforestation), floods, or the decline of trade (among others)
solution: The decline of the Harappan Civilisation (around 1900 BCE, the end of the Mature Harappan phase) is attributed by scholars to various possible causes, but no single, certain cause is agreed upon. Proposed causes include: climatic and environmental changes — such as a change in the pattern of rainfall/aridity (drying up), and deforestation and the overuse of the land; the drying up or shifting of rivers (e.g., the drying of the Saraswati/Ghaggar-Hakra, or the shifting of the Indus), which would have disrupted agriculture and settlements; floods; and the decline/disruption of trade (e.g., with Mesopotamia). (Earlier theories of an 'Aryan invasion' destroying the cities are now largely discounted.) It was probably a combination of such factors, leading to the gradual decline and abandonment of the cities. Understanding the debated causes of the Harappan decline (environmental change, river changes, etc.) is a prelims point. The decline of the Harappan Civilisation is attributed to possible causes like climatic/environmental change, the drying/shifting of rivers, floods, or the decline of trade — but no single certain cause.

stem: Our knowledge of the Harappan Civilisation comes almost entirely from __________, because their writing has not been deciphered.
options: archaeology (the material remains excavated — buildings, seals, tools, pottery, etc.)
solution: Our knowledge of the Harappan Civilisation comes almost entirely from archaeology — that is, from the study of the material remains that archaeologists have excavated: the ruins of the cities (buildings, streets, drains, the Great Bath, granaries), and the artefacts (seals, beads, pottery, tools, weights, ornaments, sculptures, bones, and so on). This is because the Harappans' own writing (their script) has not been deciphered, so we cannot read any written records they may have left — we have no readable texts telling us their history, beliefs, or names in their own words. So, unlike civilisations whose writing we can read, the Harappans are known to us almost solely through their material/archaeological remains (which archaeologists interpret). Understanding that we know the Harappans mainly through archaeology (because their script is undeciphered) is a key prelims point. Our knowledge of the Harappans comes almost entirely from archaeology, because their writing has not been deciphered.

stem: Assertion (A): We know relatively little about the political and religious life of the Harappans. Reason (R): Their script has not been deciphered, and they left no clearly-identified temples, palaces, or royal records. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that we know relatively little (with certainty) about the political and religious life of the Harappans (e.g., who ruled them, and exactly what and how they worshipped). And the reason is (R) that their script has not been deciphered — so we cannot read any written records they may have left about their rulers, laws, beliefs, or gods — and, moreover, they left no clearly-identified monumental temples, grand palaces, or royal tombs/records that would tell us plainly about their religion and rulers. Because we lack both readable writing AND clear religious/royal monuments, we are left to guess at their political and religious life from indirect archaeological clues — so R correctly explains why we know so little about these aspects (A). Understanding this (undeciphered script + no clear temples/palaces → little known about politics/religion) is a prelims point. We know little about Harappan politics/religion because their script is undeciphered and they left no clear temples, palaces, or royal records.

stem: The Harappan sites were first excavated in the 1920s under the __________ (the government body responsible for archaeology in India).
solution: The Harappan sites (Harappa and Mohenjodaro) were first excavated in the 1920s under the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) — the government body responsible for archaeological research and the conservation of monuments in India (established in 1861, with Alexander Cunningham as its first Director-General). Daya Ram Sahni excavated at Harappa and Rakhal Das (R.D.) Banerji at Mohenjodaro, and John Marshall (the Director-General of the ASI) announced the discovery of the civilisation in 1924. So the ASI conducted the pioneering excavations that revealed the Harappan Civilisation. Understanding the ASI's role (and the 1920s discovery) is a prelims point. The Harappan sites were first excavated in the 1920s under the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI).

stem: The discovery of the Harappan Civilisation was formally announced in 1924 by __________, the then Director-General of the ASI.
solution: The discovery of the Harappan Civilisation was formally announced in 1924 by John Marshall, who was then the Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI). Marshall announced (in a journal) that a hitherto-unknown ancient civilisation had been discovered at Harappa and Mohenjodaro. (The actual excavations were done by Daya Ram Sahni at Harappa and R.D. Banerji at Mohenjodaro; and Mortimer Wheeler was a later ASI Director-General who excavated Harappan sites in the 1940s.) Understanding that John Marshall announced the discovery in 1924 is a prelims point. The discovery of the Harappan Civilisation was announced in 1924 by John Marshall, the Director-General of the ASI.

stem: The Harappan Civilisation is classified as a __________ Age civilisation, because its people used tools and objects of copper and bronze (but not iron).
solution: The Harappan Civilisation is classified as a Bronze Age civilisation (it is also called a 'Chalcolithic' — copper-stone — culture). This is because its people used tools, weapons, and objects made of copper and bronze (an alloy of copper and tin), as well as stone — but they did NOT know or use iron (iron came to the subcontinent only much later). So, like the contemporary civilisations of Mesopotamia and Egypt, the Harappan Civilisation belongs to the Bronze Age. (The absence of iron is one of the features that dates and characterises it.) Understanding that the Harappans were a Bronze Age (copper/bronze-using, no iron) civilisation is a prelims point. The Harappan Civilisation is a Bronze Age civilisation — its people used copper and bronze, but not iron.

stem: The largest Harappan site discovered in India is __________ (in Haryana).
solution: Rakhigarhi, in Haryana, is the largest Harappan site discovered in India (and one of the largest of the entire civilisation). It is an extensive site that has yielded evidence of a major Harappan urban settlement. (Other important Harappan sites in India include Dholavira and Lothal in Gujarat, Kalibangan in Rajasthan, and Banawali in Haryana; the largest sites overall — including in Pakistan — are Mohenjodaro and Harappa.) Understanding that Rakhigarhi (Haryana) is the largest Harappan site in India is a prelims point. Rakhigarhi, in Haryana, is the largest Harappan site discovered in India.

stem: The main food crops grown by the Harappans included wheat and __________ (the two staple cereals).
solution: The main food crops grown by the Harappans were wheat and barley — the two staple cereals. They also cultivated pulses (like peas and lentils/gram), sesame, mustard, and, at some sites (like Lothal in Gujarat), rice and millets. Importantly, the Harappans were among the earliest people in the world to grow cotton (used for making cloth). Their agriculture (based on the fertile floodplains and, likely, some irrigation) produced the surplus that supported their cities and crafts. (Maize, coffee, and tea were not grown — maize came from the Americas much later.) Understanding the Harappan crops (wheat and barley as staples) is a prelims point. The Harappans grew wheat and barley as their staple cereals (along with pulses, sesame, mustard, and cotton).

stem: The Harappans were among the earliest people in the world to grow and use __________ (for making cloth).
solution: The Harappans were among the earliest people in the world to cultivate and use cotton (for making cloth/textiles). Evidence of cotton has been found at Harappan sites, and the Harappans are credited with being pioneers in growing cotton and making cotton cloth. (Cotton is sometimes associated with the region — the Greeks later called it 'sindon', possibly derived from 'Sindh'/Indus.) Cotton textiles may also have been among the goods the Harappans traded. So cotton cultivation is an important Harappan achievement. Understanding that the Harappans were early cotton-growers is a prelims point. The Harappans were among the earliest people in the world to grow and use cotton (for cloth).

stem: Evidence of a PLOUGHED FIELD (showing the Harappans used the plough for agriculture) was found at the site of:
solution: Evidence of a ploughed field — showing furrows in a criss-cross (grid) pattern, indicating that the Harappans ploughed the land (probably to grow two crops together) — was found at the site of Kalibangan, in Rajasthan. This is important direct evidence that the Harappans used the plough for agriculture (and terracotta models of ploughs have also been found). Kalibangan is also known for its fire altars. So the ploughed field at Kalibangan is a key piece of evidence for Harappan agriculture. Understanding this (ploughed field at Kalibangan) is a prelims point. Evidence of a ploughed field, showing the use of the plough, was found at Kalibangan (Rajasthan).

stem: The Harappans used standardised __________ (usually cubical, made of chert) for measuring, showing a system of weights.
solution: The Harappans used standardised weights for weighing/measuring goods (important for trade and exchange). These weights were usually cubical (cube-shaped) and made of a stone called chert, and they were remarkably standardised — following a regular system (the lower weights in a binary/doubling series — 1, 2, 4, 8, 16... — and the higher ones in a decimal system). The same weights/standards were used across the far-flung Harappan sites. This standardisation of weights is striking evidence of organised trade and a regulated system of measurement across the civilisation. Understanding the standardised Harappan weights (cubical chert) is a prelims point. The Harappans used standardised weights (usually cubical, made of chert), showing an organised system of weights and measurement.

stem: The Harappan site of __________ (in Gujarat) is distinctive for its use of STONE (not just brick) in construction and its elaborate water reservoirs, and it had a signboard with large script.
solution: Dholavira, a Harappan site in Gujarat (in the Rann of Kutch region), is distinctive for several reasons: it made extensive use of stone (dressed stone blocks) in its construction, not just the usual mud/baked bricks; it had elaborate, sophisticated systems of water conservation — large water reservoirs and channels (crucial in that arid region); it was divided into three parts (not just two); and it is famous for a 'signboard' — an inscription of large Harappan script signs (letters), possibly displayed on a gateway. Dholavira is thus a remarkable Harappan city, notable for its stonework and water management. Understanding these features of Dholavira is a prelims point. Dholavira (Gujarat) is distinctive for its use of stone construction, elaborate water reservoirs, and a large-script 'signboard'.

stem: The Harappan site of __________ (in Sindh) was a specialised craft/bead-making centre and, unusually, had NO citadel.
solution: Chanhudaro, a Harappan site in Sindh (Pakistan), was a small settlement that was almost exclusively devoted to craft production — including bead-making, shell-cutting, metal-working, seal-making, and weight-making. It was a specialised craft/manufacturing centre. Unusually (unlike the major cities), Chanhudaro had NO citadel (no raised, walled Citadel part) — it was a small craft town, not a large planned city with the usual Citadel/Lower Town division. So Chanhudaro is notable as a craft (especially bead-making) centre without a citadel. Understanding this (Chanhudaro = craft/bead centre, no citadel) is a prelims point. Chanhudaro (Sindh) was a specialised craft and bead-making centre that, unusually, had no citadel.

stem: The Harappans obtained raw materials for their crafts from distant regions — for example, copper (from Rajasthan/Khetri) and __________ (a blue stone, from Afghanistan).
solution: The Harappans obtained the raw materials for their crafts from various, often distant, regions — showing extensive procurement networks and trade. For example: copper from the Khetri region of Rajasthan (and from Oman); gold from Karnataka (south India); carnelian from Gujarat; shell from the coasts; steatite from various sources; tin (for making bronze) from distant regions like Afghanistan/Central Asia; and lapis lazuli — a beautiful blue semi-precious stone — from Afghanistan (Badakhshan). This procurement of materials from far and wide (some hundreds of kilometres away) reflects the reach of the Harappan economy and trade. Understanding this (raw materials from distant regions, e.g., lapis lazuli from Afghanistan) is a prelims point. The Harappans obtained raw materials from distant regions — e.g., copper from Rajasthan and lapis lazuli (a blue stone) from Afghanistan.

stem: Fire altars (suggesting some form of fire worship/ritual) have been found at Harappan sites such as Kalibangan and:
solution: Fire altars — hearths/pits that appear to have been used for some kind of ritual involving fire (fire worship or sacrifice) — have been found at Harappan sites such as Kalibangan (in Rajasthan) and Lothal (in Gujarat). The presence of these fire altars suggests that fire may have had a religious/ritual significance for (at least some of) the Harappans. (These, along with other finds like figurines and seals, are used to speculate about Harappan religion — though, since the script is undeciphered, much remains uncertain.) Understanding that fire altars were found at Kalibangan and Lothal is a prelims point. Fire altars (suggesting fire ritual/worship) have been found at Harappan sites like Kalibangan and Lothal.

stem: A famous Harappan seal depicting a seated figure surrounded by animals, which some scholars interpret as a 'proto-Shiva' (Pashupati), is called the __________ seal.
solution: The famous Harappan seal that depicts a seated figure (in a possibly yogic posture, wearing a horned headdress) surrounded by animals is called the 'Pashupati' seal (or the 'proto-Shiva' seal). Some scholars (like John Marshall) interpreted this figure as an early form ('proto') of the later Hindu god Shiva — specifically 'Pashupati' (meaning 'Lord of the Animals/Beasts'), because the figure is surrounded by animals. This interpretation suggests a possible continuity between Harappan religion and later Hinduism — but it is debated and uncertain (since the script is undeciphered, we cannot be sure). Understanding the Pashupati/proto-Shiva seal is a prelims point. The famous Harappan seal of a seated figure surrounded by animals is interpreted by some as 'Pashupati' (proto-Shiva).

stem: Numerous terracotta figurines of women, thought by some scholars to represent a __________, have been found at Harappan sites.
solution: Numerous terracotta (baked clay) figurines of women, often adorned with ornaments and elaborate headdresses, have been found at Harappan sites. Some scholars interpret these female figurines as representations of a 'Mother Goddess' — a fertility deity (associated with fertility, motherhood, and the earth) — suggesting that the Harappans may have worshipped such a goddess. (This, like other interpretations of Harappan religion, is speculative, since the script is undeciphered.) The Mother Goddess figurines are among the clues used to reconstruct Harappan religious beliefs. Understanding the Mother Goddess figurines is a prelims point. Terracotta female figurines, interpreted by some as a 'Mother Goddess' (fertility deity), have been found at Harappan sites.

stem: The stone sculpture of a bearded man (found at Mohenjodaro), often thought to represent a priest or ruler, is called the:
solution: The stone (steatite) sculpture of a bearded man, found at Mohenjodaro, is famously called the 'Priest-King'. It is a bust (head and shoulders) of a man with a beard, a headband, and a robe (shawl) decorated with a trefoil (clover-leaf) pattern draped over one shoulder. The name 'Priest-King' was given because scholars speculated the figure might represent a priest or ruler — but this is only a guess (we do not actually know who or what it represents, or whether the Harappans had priest-kings). It is one of the most famous Harappan sculptures. Understanding the 'Priest-King' sculpture is a prelims point. The stone sculpture of a bearded man from Mohenjodaro is called the 'Priest-King'.

stem: The Harappan houses were often built around a central __________, and many had their own wells and bathrooms.
solution: The Harappan houses were often built around a central courtyard (an open space in the middle of the house), with the rooms arranged around it (the courtyard was probably the centre of activities like cooking and weaving, especially in hot/dry weather). Many houses also had their own private wells (for water) and bathrooms (with drains connecting to the street drains). Notably, the houses had few or no windows/openings on the ground-floor walls facing the street (giving privacy). This arrangement (courtyard-centred houses with wells, bathrooms, and drains) reflects the comfort, privacy, and concern for water and sanitation of Harappan domestic life. Understanding the Harappan house layout (courtyard, wells, bathrooms) is a prelims point. Harappan houses were often built around a central courtyard, and many had their own wells and bathrooms.

stem: The Harappan Civilisation had extensive contact/trade with __________ (in West Asia), evidenced by Harappan seals and goods found there.
solution: The Harappan Civilisation had extensive long-distance contact and trade with Mesopotamia (the civilisation of the Tigris-Euphrates region in West Asia, modern Iraq). This is evidenced by the finding of Harappan seals, beads (like carnelian beads), and other goods at Mesopotamian sites, and by references in Mesopotamian texts to trade with a land called 'Meluhha' (identified with the Harappan region). The trade was probably conducted partly by sea (via the Persian Gulf) and involved goods like carnelian beads, cotton, timber, and other items. This Harappan-Mesopotamian trade is important evidence of the Harappans' external commercial links. Understanding the Harappan trade with Mesopotamia is a prelims point. The Harappans had extensive trade with Mesopotamia (West Asia), shown by Harappan seals and goods found there.

stem: The Harappan script was probably written from __________, based on the analysis of the signs on the seals.
solution: The Harappan script was probably written from right to left — this is deduced from the analysis of the signs on the seals (for example, from the way the signs are spaced and sometimes cramped at the left end, suggesting the writing began at the right and moved leftward). The script is pictographic (using picture-like signs), with a few hundred distinct signs, and it is found in short inscriptions (mostly on seals). But, importantly, it remains undeciphered (we cannot read it). So we know its likely direction (right to left) but not its meaning. Understanding the likely direction of the Harappan script (right to left) is a prelims point. The Harappan script was probably written from right to left.

stem: The Harappan seals are important as evidence, but the writing on them is very __________ (only a few signs per seal), which adds to the difficulty of deciphering the script.
solution: The Harappan seals carry inscriptions of the Harappan script, but the writing on them is very short (brief) — typically only a few signs (letters) per seal (the inscriptions are among the shortest of any ancient script). This brevity is one of the factors that makes deciphering the Harappan script so difficult: with only very short inscriptions (and no long texts, no bilingual inscriptions like a 'Rosetta Stone', and no known related language), scholars have too little material to crack the code. So the shortness of the inscriptions (along with the lack of a bilingual key) contributes to the script remaining undeciphered. Understanding this (short inscriptions → hard to decipher) is a prelims point. The writing on the Harappan seals is very short (a few signs each), which adds to the difficulty of deciphering the script.

stem: The theory of an 'Aryan invasion' destroying the Harappan cities (proposed by Mortimer Wheeler based on some skeletons at Mohenjodaro) is now:
options: largely rejected/discounted by most scholars (the evidence does not support a violent invasion as the cause of decline)
solution: The theory of an 'Aryan invasion' destroying the Harappan cities — proposed by the archaeologist Mortimer Wheeler, who pointed to some unburied skeletons found at Mohenjodaro as evidence of a 'massacre' by invading Aryans — is now largely rejected/discounted by most scholars. Later analysis showed that the skeletons did not all belong to the same period and did not really provide evidence of a single violent massacre/invasion; and the decline of the Harappan Civilisation is now attributed to gradual processes (environmental and climatic changes, the drying/shifting of rivers, the decline of trade, etc.) rather than a sudden invasion. So the 'Aryan invasion → destruction' theory is no longer accepted as the explanation for the Harappan decline. Understanding that this theory is now discounted is a prelims point. The 'Aryan invasion destroying the Harappan cities' theory (Wheeler) is now largely rejected by most scholars.

stem: The Harappan Civilisation extended over a very large area — from Sutkagendor in the west to __________ in the east, making it one of the largest of the ancient civilisations by area.
solution: The Harappan Civilisation extended over a very large area — much larger than the contemporary civilisations of Egypt and Mesopotamia by area. It stretched roughly from Sutkagendor (near the Makran coast, in Balochistan) in the west to Alamgirpur (in western Uttar Pradesh, near Delhi) in the east; and from Manda (in Jammu) in the north to Daimabad (in Maharashtra) in the south. This vast extent (covering much of the north-western subcontinent — parts of present-day Pakistan and north-western/western India) is remarkable, and the uniformity of its culture (bricks, weights, seals, town planning) over such a large area is one of its striking features. Understanding the wide extent of the civilisation (west to east: Sutkagendor to Alamgirpur) is a prelims point. The Harappan Civilisation extended from Sutkagendor in the west to Alamgirpur (near Delhi) in the east — a very large area.

stem: Reconstructing the religious beliefs of the Harappans is difficult and speculative mainly because:
options: their script is undeciphered, so we cannot read their own descriptions, and we must guess from objects (figurines, seals) whose meaning is uncertain
there are too many written records
solution: Reconstructing the religious beliefs of the Harappans is difficult and speculative mainly because their script is undeciphered — so we cannot read any of the Harappans' own words/descriptions of their religion (their gods, rituals, or beliefs). Instead, scholars must guess about Harappan religion from indirect archaeological objects — such as the terracotta 'Mother Goddess' figurines, the 'Pashupati'/proto-Shiva seal, fire altars, depictions of trees/animals on seals, and so on — but the meaning and significance of these objects are uncertain (we are interpreting/guessing what they meant to the Harappans). This is why any reconstruction of Harappan religion is tentative and debated. Understanding why Harappan religion is hard to reconstruct (undeciphered script + uncertain-meaning objects) is a prelims point. Harappan religion is hard to reconstruct because the script is undeciphered, so we must guess from objects (figurines, seals) whose meaning is uncertain.

stem: The presence of standardised bricks, weights, seals, and town planning ACROSS the far-flung Harappan sites suggests:
options: a high degree of uniformity, standardisation, and possibly some central control/authority over the civilisation
solution: The presence of the same standardised features — bricks (of a fixed ratio), weights (cubical chert, in a regular system), seals (of a common style and script), and town planning (grid layout, Citadel/Lower Town, drainage) — across the far-flung Harappan sites (spread over a vast area) suggests a high degree of uniformity and standardisation throughout the civilisation. This remarkable uniformity, in turn, suggests that there was some kind of central organisation, control, or shared authority/system regulating the civilisation (though we do not know exactly what — whether a single state, a group of rulers, or a shared cultural/economic system) — since such uniform standards over such a wide area do not arise by chance. So the standardisation points to organisation and possibly central control. Understanding this inference (uniformity → standardisation/central control) is a prelims point. The standardised bricks, weights, seals, and planning across the Harappan sites suggest a high degree of uniformity and possibly some central control/authority.

stem: Archaeologists study the __________ (plant and animal remains, like charred grains and bones) at Harappan sites to reconstruct what the people ate and reared.
solution: Archaeologists study the subsistence remains — the plant remains (archaeobotanical remains, like charred/burnt grains and seeds) and the animal remains (faunal remains, like animal bones) — found at Harappan sites, in order to reconstruct what the Harappans ate and what animals they reared and hunted. For example, finding charred grains of wheat and barley tells us what crops they grew and ate; and studying animal bones tells us which animals they kept (cattle, sheep, goats, buffalo, pigs) or hunted (and whether the bones show cut marks, etc.). This scientific study of plant and animal remains (by archaeobotanists and archaeozoologists) is how the Harappans' diet and food economy are reconstructed. Understanding that subsistence (plant/animal) remains reveal the Harappan diet is a prelims point. Archaeologists study the plant and animal remains (charred grains, bones) at Harappan sites to reconstruct what the people ate and reared.

stem: The Harappans reared domesticated animals such as cattle, sheep, goats, and buffalo. The evidence for the __________ in the Harappan Civilisation is debated/uncertain.
solution: The Harappans reared several domesticated animals — including cattle (which seem to have been especially important), sheep, goats, buffalo, and pigs (and they knew the elephant and camel). However, the evidence for the horse in the (mature) Harappan Civilisation is debated and uncertain — clear, well-attested horse remains are rare/absent at mature Harappan sites, and the horse does not feature on the Harappan seals. (This has been a point of scholarly and even political debate, e.g., in connection with the 'Aryan' question.) So, while the Harappans' cattle, sheep, goats, and buffalo are well-attested, the horse's presence is questionable/debated. Understanding that the horse's presence is debated is a prelims-relevant point. The Harappans reared cattle, sheep, goats, and buffalo, but the evidence for the horse is debated/uncertain.

stem: The Harappan pottery was typically __________, often decorated with black designs.
solution: The characteristic Harappan pottery was typically 'red ware' — pottery with a red surface (red slip) — which was often decorated/painted with designs in black (black-on-red ware). The designs included geometric patterns, plants (like the pipal leaf), animals, and other motifs. The pottery was well-made (often wheel-turned) and fired. This distinctive black-on-red pottery is one of the identifying artefacts of the Harappan Civilisation (helping archaeologists recognise Harappan sites). Understanding the Harappan pottery (red ware with black designs) is a prelims point. Harappan pottery was typically red ware, decorated with black-painted designs.

stem: The way archaeologists RECOVER and interpret Harappan artefacts (deciding what an object was used for, or what it meant) involves a lot of __________, especially for objects with no obvious use.
options: careful reasoning and interpretation (and sometimes guesswork)
solution: The way archaeologists recover and interpret Harappan artefacts — deciding what an object was used for (its function), or what it meant to the people (its significance) — involves a great deal of careful reasoning and interpretation (and, for many objects, an element of educated guesswork/speculation). This is because the Harappans left no readable written records to tell us directly; so, for objects whose use is not obvious, archaeologists must infer/interpret — using clues like the object's shape, material, context (where it was found), comparisons with known objects, and analogies — and different scholars may interpret the same object differently (e.g., is a structure a 'granary' or something else? Is a figure a 'goddess' or a toy?). So interpreting the archaeological evidence is a careful, reasoned, but often uncertain process. Understanding that interpreting Harappan artefacts involves careful reasoning/interpretation (not certainty) is a key prelims-relevant point. Interpreting Harappan artefacts (their use or meaning) involves careful reasoning and interpretation — and often guesswork — especially for objects with no obvious use.

stem: Assertion (A): The Harappan Civilisation extended over a much larger area than contemporary Egypt or Mesopotamia. Reason (R): Harappan sites are spread across a vast region from Balochistan and Sindh to Gujarat, Rajasthan, and the western Ganga-Yamuna region. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the Harappan Civilisation extended over a much larger area than the contemporary civilisations of Egypt or Mesopotamia. And the reason is (R) that Harappan sites are indeed spread across a vast region — from Balochistan (Sutkagendor) and Sindh in the west and south-west, through Punjab, Gujarat, Rajasthan, and Haryana, to the western Ganga-Yamuna region (Alamgirpur) in the east (and from Jammu in the north to Maharashtra in the south). Because the sites cover such an enormous geographical spread, the civilisation was indeed larger in area than Egypt or Mesopotamia — so R (the wide spread of sites) correctly explains/supports A (the large area). Understanding this (the Harappan Civilisation's vast extent) is a prelims point. The Harappan Civilisation was larger in area than Egypt or Mesopotamia because its sites spread across a vast region from Balochistan/Sindh to Gujarat, Rajasthan, and the western Ganga-Yamuna area.

stem: The Harappan Civilisation belonged to the __________ Age, as its people used copper and bronze but not iron.
solution: The Harappan Civilisation was a Bronze Age civilisation; its people used copper and bronze, but iron was not yet known to them.

stem: Mohenjodaro is located in the __________ province of present-day Pakistan.
solution: Mohenjodaro is located in the Sindh province of present-day Pakistan, on the Indus river.

stem: The Harappan seals were mostly made of a soft stone called:
solution: Harappan seals were usually made of steatite, a soft stone, and engraved with animals and script.

stem: The most frequently depicted animal on Harappan seals is the:
solution: The 'unicorn' — a one-horned mythical animal — is the most commonly depicted motif on Harappan seals.

stem: The lower town of a Harappan city, where most people lived, is generally distinguished from the __________, the higher walled part.
solution: Harappan cities were divided into a higher, walled 'Citadel' and a larger 'Lower Town' where most people lived.

stem: The Great Bath at Mohenjodaro was made watertight by using __________ between the bricks.
solution: The Great Bath was made watertight using finely fitted bricks and a layer of natural tar (bitumen) to prevent seepage.

stem: The Harappans used a standardised system of weights that were generally made of:
solution: Harappan weights were usually cubical and made of chert, a hard stone, showing a standardised measurement system.

stem: The lower denominations of Harappan weights were in a __________ system.
solution: The lower Harappan weights followed a binary system (1, 2, 4, 8, 16...), while higher weights followed a decimal system.

stem: The Harappan site notable for its dockyard, suggesting maritime trade, is:
solution: Lothal, in Gujarat, is notable for its dockyard, indicating it was a port involved in maritime trade.

stem: The largest Harappan site in India, located in Haryana, is:
solution: Rakhigarhi in Haryana is the largest Harappan site discovered in India.

stem: The Harappan site in Gujarat distinctive for its extensive use of STONE and elaborate water reservoirs is:
solution: Dholavira, in Gujarat, is distinctive for its stone architecture and elaborate water-harvesting reservoirs, and had a large signboard with script.

stem: The Harappan site of Chanhudaro was unusual because it:
options: was a specialised craft (bead-making) centre with no citadel
solution: Chanhudaro was a small settlement specialised in craft production (bead-making, shell-working, etc.) and, unusually, had no citadel.

stem: Evidence of a ploughed field, showing use of the plough, was found at the Harappan site of:
solution: A ploughed field was found at Kalibangan (in Rajasthan), evidence that the Harappans used the plough for agriculture.

stem: The Harappans imported the blue stone lapis lazuli for their crafts from:
solution: Lapis lazuli, a blue stone used in Harappan crafts, was obtained from Afghanistan.

stem: Harappan copper was largely obtained from the Khetri region of:
solution: Copper was obtained from the Khetri region of Rajasthan (as well as from Oman/Baluchistan).

stem: The Harappans made beautiful beads especially from a reddish semi-precious stone called:
solution: Carnelian, a reddish semi-precious stone, was a favourite material for Harappan bead-making.

stem: Mesopotamian texts refer to a distant trading land called '__________', identified with the Harappan region.
solution: Mesopotamian texts mention 'Meluhha', which many scholars identify with the Harappan (Indus) region.

stem: In Mesopotamian trade references, Dilmun and Magan were intermediary trading stations; Dilmun is generally identified with:
solution: Dilmun is generally identified with the island of Bahrain, an intermediary in the trade between Meluhha (Harappa) and Mesopotamia.

stem: The famous bronze statuette made by the lost-wax technique, depicting a girl, is the:
solution: The 'Dancing Girl' is the famous bronze statuette from Mohenjodaro, made using the lost-wax (cire perdue) technique.

stem: The stone sculpture from Mohenjodaro thought to represent a priest or ruler is called the:
solution: The bearded stone figure from Mohenjodaro is conventionally called the 'Priest-King', though its actual role is uncertain.

stem: The seal depicting a seated cross-legged figure surrounded by animals, interpreted by some as 'proto-Shiva', is the:
solution: The Pashupati seal shows a seated figure surrounded by animals, interpreted by some (like Marshall) as a 'proto-Shiva'.

stem: The Harappan script is described as a __________ script (each sign standing for a sound/word), and it remains undeciphered.
solution: The Harappan script is a pictographic/logo-syllabic script; it remains undeciphered, and its language is unknown.

stem: The Harappan script was most likely written from:
solution: Analysis of the seals suggests the Harappan script was generally written from right to left.

stem: The Harappan Civilisation was discovered and its sites first excavated in the 1920s under the:
solution: Harappan sites were first excavated in the 1920s under the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI).

stem: The discovery of the Harappan Civilisation was formally announced in 1924 by John Marshall, who was then the:
solution: John Marshall, Director-General of the ASI, announced the discovery of the Harappan Civilisation to the world in 1924.

stem: The two staple food-grain crops of the Harappans were wheat and:
solution: Wheat and barley were the two main staple cereals grown by the Harappans.

stem: The Harappans were among the earliest people in the world to grow __________ for making cloth.
solution: The Harappans were among the earliest people in the world to cultivate cotton for making cloth.

stem: Fire altars, suggesting a form of fire ritual, have been found at Harappan sites like Kalibangan and:
solution: Fire altars have been found at Kalibangan and Lothal, suggesting some form of fire ritual/worship.

stem: Numerous terracotta figurines of women found at Harappan sites are interpreted by some scholars as representing a:
solution: Many terracotta female figurines are interpreted by some scholars as representing a 'Mother Goddess', though this is debated.

stem: The Harappan drainage system was remarkable because:
options: house drains connected to covered street drains, showing careful planning of the whole city
waste was thrown in the streets
solution: Harappan house drains connected to covered street drains, reflecting a carefully planned, city-wide sanitation system — rare in the ancient world.

stem: The Harappan houses commonly had their own __________, showing attention to water supply and hygiene.
solution: Many Harappan houses had their own wells and bathrooms, reflecting attention to water supply and hygiene.

stem: The standardisation of bricks, weights, seals and town planning across far-flung Harappan sites suggests:
options: some form of central authority or shared cultural/administrative system over a large area
solution: The uniformity of bricks, weights, seals and planning across distant sites suggests some form of central authority or a shared administrative/cultural system.

stem: Unlike Egypt and Mesopotamia, the Harappan Civilisation lacks clear evidence of:
options: grand temples, royal tombs and palaces of kings
solution: The Harappans left no clearly identified grand temples, royal tombs or palaces, making their political and religious organisation uncertain.

stem: The Harappan Civilisation extended over a vast area, from Sutkagendor in the west to __________ in the east.
solution: The Harappan Civilisation extended from Sutkagendor (Balochistan) in the west to Alamgirpur (western UP) in the east, one of the largest ancient civilisations by area.

stem: The theory that an 'Aryan invasion' destroyed the Harappan cities (proposed by Mortimer Wheeler) is now:
solution: The 'Aryan invasion' theory of Harappan destruction is now largely rejected; the skeletal evidence does not support a single massacre.

stem: Which of the following is a proposed cause of the decline of the Harappan Civilisation (around 1900 BCE)?
options: climate/environmental change, drying up or shifting of rivers, deforestation, or decline of trade
solution: Proposed causes of the decline include climatic/environmental change, the drying up or shifting of rivers, deforestation, floods, and the decline of trade — but no single cause is proven.

stem: Harappan pottery was typically __________, decorated with black designs.
solution: Harappan pottery was typically red ware decorated with black painted designs (red-and-black ware).

stem: Archaeologists study the __________ at Harappan sites — charred grains, seeds and animal bones — to reconstruct diet and subsistence.
solution: Archaeobotanical (plant) and faunal (animal-bone) remains are studied to reconstruct what the Harappans ate and the animals they reared.

stem: The presence of the __________ in the Harappan Civilisation is debated and uncertain among scholars.
solution: Evidence for the horse in the Harappan Civilisation is debated and uncertain, unlike the well-attested cattle, sheep, goats and buffalo.

stem: A large brick structure at the Mohenjodaro Citadel, thought (though debated) to have been used for storing grain, is called the:
solution: A large brick structure at the Citadel is conventionally called the 'Granary' or warehouse, thought to have stored grain, though its function is debated.

stem: Reconstructing Harappan religious beliefs is difficult and speculative mainly because:
options: the script is undeciphered and there are no clearly identified religious texts, temples or records
solution: Because the script is undeciphered and no religious texts, temples or records are clearly identified, reconstructing Harappan religion is largely speculative.

stem: Interpreting the use and meaning of Harappan artefacts (especially objects with no obvious function) involves a lot of:
solution: Since the script is undeciphered, archaeologists must rely heavily on inference and reasoned guesswork to interpret Harappan artefacts.

stem: Our knowledge of the Harappan Civilisation comes almost entirely from:
options: archaeological/material evidence (artefacts, structures), because the writing is undeciphered
solution: Because the Harappan script is undeciphered, our knowledge comes almost entirely from archaeological/material evidence — artefacts and structures.

stem: The Harappan Civilisation is also called the 'Indus Valley Civilisation' and, more broadly, the __________ Civilisation.
solution: It is called the Indus Valley Civilisation, and (because many sites lie along the now-dry Ghaggar-Hakra/Saraswati) sometimes the Indus-Saraswati or Harappan Civilisation.

stem: Assertion (A): We know relatively little about the political and religious life of the Harappans. Reason (R): Their script has not been deciphered, and they left no clearly identified temples, palaces or royal records. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true and R correctly explains A
A is true but R is false
solution: Both are true and R explains A: the undeciphered script and the absence of clear temples, palaces or records leave their politics and religion largely unknown.

stem: Assertion (A): The Harappan Civilisation extended over a larger area than contemporary Egypt or Mesopotamia. Reason (R): Harappan sites spread across a vast region from Balochistan and Sindh to Gujarat, Rajasthan and the western Ganga-Yamuna region. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true and R correctly explains A
A is true but R is false
solution: Both are true and R explains A: its vast spread across Balochistan, Sindh, Gujarat, Rajasthan and the western Ganga-Yamuna region made it larger in area than contemporary Egypt or Mesopotamia.

stem: Which of the following BEST captures the central message of the chapter 'Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation'?
options: The Harappans left detailed written histories

The Harappan Civilisation was a remarkable, sophisticated urban Bronze-Age culture known mainly through archaeology, whose planning, crafts and trade impress us, though much about its politics, religion and decline remains uncertain
solution: The chapter concludes that the Harappan Civilisation was a sophisticated urban Bronze-Age culture — notable for town planning, crafts and trade — reconstructed mainly through archaeology, while much about its politics, religion and decline remains uncertain.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation' is that:
options: The Harappan Civilisation (c. 2600–1900 BCE) was one of the world's earliest and most remarkable urban civilisations — with planned cities, advanced drainage, standardised bricks, crafts (beads, seals), trade (even with Mesopotamia), and a script — reconstructed by archaeologists from its material remains ('bricks, beads, and bones'), though much about it (its undeciphered script, its rulers, its decline) remains a mystery
The Harappan script is fully understood
solution: The chapter conveys that the Harappan (Indus Valley) Civilisation — flourishing in its Mature phase around 2600–1900 BCE in the north-western part of the Indian subcontinent — was one of the world's earliest and most remarkable urban (Bronze Age) civilisations. It highlights its distinctive features: carefully planned cities (like Mohenjodaro and Harappa), laid out on a grid pattern and divided into a raised, walled 'Citadel' (with structures like the Great Bath and the granary) and a 'Lower Town'; an advanced, well-planned drainage/sanitation system; the use of standardised (baked) bricks of a fixed ratio; a flourishing economy of agriculture, skilled craft production (especially beads and ornaments, seals, pottery, and metalwork — including the famous 'Dancing Girl' bronze), and long-distance trade (including with Mesopotamia, the land they may have called 'Meluhha'); characteristic seals (of steatite, engraved with animals like the 'unicorn' and with script); and a system of writing that, however, remains undeciphered. It notes the puzzling features — the absence of clear temples, palaces, or royal tombs (leaving the nature of their rulers/religion uncertain) — and the debated, uncertain causes of the civilisation's decline around 1900 BCE (environmental/climatic change, the drying or shifting of rivers, floods, the decline of trade). Crucially, it emphasises that all this knowledge is reconstructed by archaeologists from the material remains — the 'bricks, beads, and bones' (the buildings, the artefacts, and the skeletal/animal remains) — since the Harappans' own writing cannot yet be read, so that much about them still remains a mystery. Understanding the features, economy, script, and decline of the Harappan Civilisation, and how it is reconstructed from archaeology, is the central concern of this chapter. The Harappan Civilisation was one of the world's earliest, most remarkable urban civilisations — of planned cities, drainage, crafts, trade, and an undeciphered script — reconstructed from its material remains, with much still a mystery.
